title: Visiting the sites
hookLine: gurdwaras now mark Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira

lines: A WHITE DOME, A SAFFRON FLAG.
GROUND WITH A NAME IN MEMORY.
cards: Flat fields. Wheat, or mustard in its season, running to the edge of sight. An irrigation channel, a dirt road, a tractor parked by a wall.
And in the middle of it, a white building with a dome and a tall flagpole, the saffron Nishan Sahib lifting in the wind. If you didn't know the story, you'd see a village gurdwara like any other.
But this ground has a name in Sikh memory. Today: visiting the sites.

teach.b: The first place is Kahnuwan, near the marshes where, a few weeks back, families and riders were trapped in the smaller holocaust, the chhota ghallughara. Ghallughara means a great destruction.
Chhota means small, though nothing about it was small to those who lived it. Today a gurdwara stands there, and Sikhs come to remember.
The second is Kup Rahira, where the Khalsa made a moving ring around its families and the great holocaust, the vadda ghallughara, fell on them.
A gurdwara marks that ground too. Now notice what stands at the heart of each site. Not a battle trophy.
Not a wall of grievance. A gurdwara: the Guru Granth Sahib opened, hymns sung, and a langar feeding anyone who walks in. The memorial is a working kitchen.
That fits this whole week: memory pointed at courage, the pot before the sword. And the sites hold a quiet lesson.
The fields came back. Crops grow right up to the gurdwara walls. A child can grow up within sight of it and learn the story from the person who serves them tea there.
The places hold what happened, so the people who live there don't carry it alone.
This week: Rattan Singh Bhangu, remembering without hatred, the Budha Dal today, daily life on horseback, langar in hard times, the Khalsa shall rule, and visiting the sites.

how: Gurdwaras stand at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira; Sikhs visit to pray and remember the two ghallugharas, and the anniversaries are marked there with readings, kirtan and langar.

o: a gurdwara built where a battle was won
a great destruction, a massacre in Sikh memory
a ring of riders guarding the families

games.q: two places, two memories — tap the pairs.

s: the sites are marked only with battle monuments
at the heart of each is a gurdwara, with scripture, song and a langar.
the land around the sites was left empty
the fields came back, and crops grow right up to the gurdwara walls.
chhota ghallughara means the smaller holocaust
chhota means small; ghallughara, a great destruction.

games.q: you're one of the Sikhs deciding how to mark the ground at Kup Rahira, where the great holocaust fell. what do you build?
o: a victory pillar for the survivors.
a gurdwara, with the Granth, hymns and a langar.
nothing; let the fields cover it.
games.why: a gurdwara stands there. the memorial is a working kitchen and a place to sing.

practice: If you have a phone nearby, open a map and find Kahnuwan or Kup Rahira; zoom in until you see the fields and roads, then put it down and close your eyes.
Hold that ordinary ground and what tradition says happened there, or simply picture the white dome in the fields. If you pray, say Waheguru softly on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: ghallughara, the great destruction; gurdwaras now stand at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira, where the two ghallugharas fell, with scripture, song and a kitchen. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for ghallughara, a great destruction, the word Sikhs use for the two holocausts.

carryVoice: Your line: the places remember. Where it happened, a kitchen now feeds whoever comes. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.
